blocks.text:
Design an Airline Management System (the seat-booking core of it) that lets passengers book a seat on a flight by seat class (ECONOMY, BUSINESS), assigns a specific physical seat when one is free, and prices the fare dynamically based on demand: the more of a class is already sold, the higher the fare for the next booking. When a class is completely sold out, additional passengers can be placed on a waitlist (bounded overbooking) instead of being turned away immediately, and are automatically promoted into any seat that later becomes free through a cancellation.

  • Actors: Passenger (books, cancels), AirlineBookingService (the core orchestrator).
  • Scope: a single flight with multiple seat classes, demand-based fares, per-class FIFO waitlists, cancellation with automatic waitlist promotion.

This differs from Movie Ticket Booking (which locks a customer-chosen seat) and Concert Ticketing (which is capacity-only, no specific seats) by combining specific seat assignment with demand-based pricing and a waitlist that activates only once physical seats run out.
The system must support the following core capabilities:

items: Seat inventory: register seats for a flight, grouped by seat class (ECONOMY, BUSINESS).
Booking: a passenger requests a seat class; the system assigns the first available seat in that class.
Dynamic pricing: the fare charged depends on how much of that class is already sold at booking time.
Waitlist: if no seat is free, the passenger joins a per-class FIFO waitlist, bounded by an overbooking limit.
Cancellation: cancelling a confirmed booking frees its seat and automatically promotes the longest-waiting waitlisted passenger, if any.
Rejection: if both the class and its waitlist are full, the booking is rejected with a clear reason.

blocks.text: Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: supporting many flights and seat classes must not require touching existing booking logic.
Extensibility: new pricing tiers or seat classes should plug in without rewriting the service.
Maintainability: pricing, notification, and seat-creation concerns are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: seat lookup and booking are O(1) or O(seats-in-class) via in-memory maps.
Thread safety: two passengers booking the last seat of a class concurrently must not both succeed.

blocks.text: Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: Can a passenger pick a specific seat (window/aisle), or is any free seat in the class acceptable?
Should the waitlist be per-class, or should a full BUSINESS request ever fall back to ECONOMY?
Should the fare be locked at booking time, or recomputed if the passenger is later promoted from a waitlist?
Is overbooking allowed at all, or must the airline strictly never sell more than physical capacity?
Should partial refunds be modeled on cancellation, or is refund policy out of scope?

blocks.text: To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: The system assigns the first available seat in the requested class automatically. Passenger-chosen exact seat selection is deliberately out of scope here, since that mechanic is already covered in depth by the Movie Ticket Booking System design.
Waitlisted bookings are not charged a fare until they are promoted to an actual seat; the fare is computed fresh at promotion time using the demand at that moment.
Overbooking is modeled as a bounded per-class waitlist (a fixed extra capacity), not unlimited overselling.
Cancellation refund policy, fuel-level fare adjustments, and multi-leg connecting flights are noted as future extensions, not implemented.

blocks.text: The design centers on five core entities:

metadata.alt: Core entities: Flight, Seat, SeatClass, Passenger, Booking, Waitlist

items: Flight: owns a set of seats and a per-class waitlist.
Seat: a physical seat with a class and a status (AVAILABLE, BOOKED).
SeatClass: an enum (ECONOMY, BUSINESS) driving the base fare.
Passenger: the person booking travel.
Booking: ties a passenger to a seat class, possibly a specific seat, a fare, and a status.

blocks.text: These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: A flight has many seats and a per-class waitlist; a passenger makes many bookings; a booking references at most one seat or one waitlist slot

items: Flight to Seat is one-to-many.
Flight to Waitlist is one-to-many, one queue per seat class.
Passenger to Booking is one-to-many.
Booking to Seat is zero-or-one (a waitlisted booking has no seat yet).

blocks.text: Three patterns keep pricing, notification, and seat creation decoupled from the core service.
Why needed: fares depend on how full a class is, and that demand curve is a business rule that changes independently of the booking workflow.

Why it is the best fit: a new pricing model (seasonal surcharge, loyalty discount) is a new class implementing the same interface, with zero changes to AirlineBookingService. What it solves: it isolates a frequently-tuned business rule (pricing) from stable orchestration logic.
Why needed: confirmations, waitlisting, cancellations, and promotions are all events other parts of a real system would want to react to.

metadata.alt: BookingObserver interface notified by AirlineBookingService on every lifecycle event

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: AirlineBookingService does not need to know who is listening. What it solves: it decouples the core booking workflow from side effects like email and SMS.
Why needed: seat id generation per class should not be scattered across setup code.
Why it is the best fit: configuring a new flight becomes a couple of factory calls. What it solves: centralizes id-generation rules so they cannot drift or collide.
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: Seat: attributes seatId, seatClass, status; responsibility: track whether one physical seat is free.
SeatFactory: method createSeats(flight, seatClass, count); responsibility: generate correctly-prefixed seat ids.
Booking: attributes bookingId, passengerId, seatId, seatClass, fare, status; responsibility: capture one booking end-to-end, confirmed or waitlisted.
AirlineBookingService: the orchestrator; responsibility: find or waitlist a seat, compute fares, process cancellations and promotions, and notify observers.

blocks.text: Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: FlightPricingStrategy and BookingObserver interfaces with their key methods

items: FlightPricingStrategy: calculateFare(seatClass, soldCount, capacity): abstracts away exactly how a fare is derived.
BookingObserver: onBookingConfirmed / onBookingWaitlisted / onBookingCancelled / onWaitlistPromoted: abstracts away who reacts to lifecycle events.

blocks.text: Three flows below cover a confirmed booking with demand pricing, a waitlisted booking, and a cancellation that auto-promotes a waitlisted passenger.

metadata.alt: Bob books ECONOMY and is charged the higher demand tier since one seat is already sold
Carol requests ECONOMY after both seats are sold and joins the waitlist
Alice cancels her booking, freeing a seat that Carol is automatically promoted into

blocks.text: The end-to-end happy path, alongside its waitlist and cancellation branches, looks like this:

metadata.alt: Book, check availability, assign or waitlist, cancel, promote

items: Happy path: book → seat found → compute fare from current demand → mark BOOKED → CONFIRMED.
Waitlist path: book → no seat found → waitlist has room → join FIFO queue → WAITLISTED.
Cancellation path: cancel → free seat → if waitlist non-empty, promote the longest-waiting entry into the freed seat.

blocks.text: The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: bookSeat(passengerId, seatClass): assigns a free seat and computes its fare, or joins the waitlist, or throws if both are full.
cancelBooking(bookingId): frees a confirmed booking's seat (or removes a waitlisted entry) and triggers waitlist promotion if applicable.

blocks.text: Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: SeatClassFullException: no seat is free and the waitlist for that class is also at capacity.
InvalidBookingException: an unknown seat class or a non-positive count during setup.
BookingNotFoundException: cancelBooking is called with an unknown or already-cancelled booking id.

blocks.text: The critical race is two passengers booking the last available seat in a class at the same moment.

metadata.alt: Two threads racing for the last ECONOMY seat; synchronization ensures only one wins and the other falls to the waitlist

blocks.text: Synchronizing the seat-search-and-mark step per flight ensures the check and the status update happen atomically, so only one booking can ever claim a given seat, and the loser is correctly waitlisted rather than also confirmed.
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A new pricing scheme (seasonal surcharge, loyalty discount) is a new FlightPricingStrategy implementation, swapped in without touching AirlineBookingService.
A new notification channel (SMS, push) is a new BookingObserver implementation.
A new seat class (PREMIUM_ECONOMY) is a new enum value plus a base fare entry, not a structural change.
Passenger-chosen exact seats can be layered on top by adding an overload that targets a specific seatId instead of just a class.
Single Responsibility: Seat tracks state, FlightPricingStrategy computes fares, BookingObserver reacts to events, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new pricing or notification behavior extends via new classes, not edits to AirlineBookingService.
Liskov Substitution: any FlightPricingStrategy or BookingObserver implementation can replace another without breaking the service.
Interface Segregation: BookingObserver exposes only the four lifecycle callbacks a listener actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: AirlineBookingService depends on the FlightPricingStrategy and BookingObserver interfaces, not concrete classes.
Booking when both the class and its waitlist are completely full throws SeatClassFullException.
Cancelling a waitlisted (not yet seated) booking simply removes it from the queue, no seat to free.
Cancelling the same booking twice throws BookingNotFoundException on the second call.
A promoted waitlist passenger is charged the fare current at promotion time, which may differ from what it would have been at original request time.
bookSeat: O(seats-in-class) to scan for a free seat, or O(1) with a per-class free-seat pool.
cancelBooking: O(1) to free the seat plus O(1) to pop the head of the waitlist queue.
Space: O(seats + bookings + waitlisted) held in memory.

blocks.text: A relational schema mirrors the in-memory model directly, with foreign keys enforcing referential integrity:

metadata.alt: ER diagram: Flight, Seat, Passenger, Booking

items: An index on Seat(flightId, seatClass, status) speeds up the "find a free seat in this class" query.
A separate Waitlist table (flightId, seatClass, bookingId, position) would back the FIFO queue in a persistent deployment.
Support passenger-chosen exact seats layered on top of the class-based assignment.
Model multi-leg connecting flights as a sequence of bookings tied together.
Add partial-refund tiers based on how close to departure a cancellation happens.
In a distributed deployment, move seat-status locking to a database-level row lock or a distributed lock rather than in-process synchronization.

from enum import Enum

# Seat class drives the base fare.
class SeatClass(Enum):
    ECONOMY = "ECONOMY"   # cheaper, larger capacity
    BUSINESS = "BUSINESS" # pricier, smaller capacity

# Lifecycle status of a single seat.
class SeatStatus(Enum):
    AVAILABLE = "AVAILABLE"  # free to be booked
    BOOKED = "BOOKED"        # currently assigned to a passenger

# A single physical seat on a flight.
class Seat:
    def __init__(self, seat_id, seat_class):
        self.seat_id = seat_id       # unique id, e.g. E1
        self.seat_class = seat_class # pricing/class tier
        self.status = SeatStatus.AVAILABLE  # new seats start free

    def is_available(self):
        return self.status == SeatStatus.AVAILABLE  # convenience check

# Creates seats with class-prefixed ids for a flight.
class SeatFactory:
    def __init__(self):
        self.counters = {}  # prefix -> count so far

    def create_seats(self, seat_class, count):
        prefix = "E" if seat_class == SeatClass.ECONOMY else "B"  # pick prefix by class
        created = []                                                # result list
        for _ in range(count):                                      # create 'count' seats
            n = self.counters.get(prefix, 0) + 1                      # next number for this prefix
            self.counters[prefix] = n                                  # remember it
            created.append(Seat(f"{prefix}{n}", seat_class))           # e.g. E1
        return created  # hand back the new seats

# Strategy interface: how a fare is computed from current demand.
class FlightPricingStrategy:
    def calculate_fare(self, seat_class, sold_count, capacity):
        raise NotImplementedError  # concrete strategies must implement this

# Demand-based pricing: higher fare as a class fills up.
class DemandBasedPricingStrategy(FlightPricingStrategy):
    def _base_fare(self, seat_class):
        return 100.0 if seat_class == SeatClass.ECONOMY else 300.0  # base fare per class

    def calculate_fare(self, seat_class, sold_count, capacity):
        base = self._base_fare(seat_class)          # starting fare
        sold_ratio = sold_count / capacity            # how full the class is before this booking
        if sold_ratio < 0.5:                            # low demand tier
            multiplier = 1.0
        elif sold_ratio < 0.8:                           # medium demand tier
            multiplier = 1.2
        else:                                             # high demand tier
            multiplier = 1.5
        return base * multiplier  # final fare

# A person booking travel.
class Passenger:
    def __init__(self, passenger_id, name):
        self.passenger_id = passenger_id  # unique id
        self.name = name                   # display name

# A single booking, confirmed or waitlisted.
class Booking:
    def __init__(self, booking_id, passenger_id, seat_class):
        self.booking_id = booking_id      # unique id
        self.passenger_id = passenger_id  # who booked it
        self.seat_id = None                 # assigned seat, None while waitlisted
        self.seat_class = seat_class       # requested class
        self.fare = 0.0                     # charged fare, 0 while waitlisted
        self.status = "PENDING"             # set properly right after construction

# Observer interface: reacts to booking lifecycle events.
class BookingObserver:
    def on_booking_confirmed(self, booking): raise NotImplementedError
    def on_booking_waitlisted(self, booking): raise NotImplementedError
    def on_booking_cancelled(self, booking): raise NotImplementedError
    def on_waitlist_promoted(self, booking): raise NotImplementedError

# Simple observer that prints events to the console.
class ConsoleBookingObserver(BookingObserver):
    def on_booking_confirmed(self, booking):
        print(f"Booking {booking.booking_id} confirmed for {booking.passenger_id}, seat {booking.seat_id}, fare {booking.fare}")

    def on_booking_waitlisted(self, booking):
        print(f"Booking {booking.booking_id} waitlisted for {booking.passenger_id}")

    def on_booking_cancelled(self, booking):
        print(f"Booking {booking.booking_id} cancelled for {booking.passenger_id}")

    def on_waitlist_promoted(self, booking):
        print(f"Booking {booking.booking_id} promoted for {booking.passenger_id}, seat {booking.seat_id}, fare {booking.fare}")

# Custom exceptions for the realistic failure modes.
class SeatClassFullException(Exception): pass
class InvalidBookingException(Exception): pass
class BookingNotFoundException(Exception): pass

# The core orchestrator tying every piece together.
class AirlineBookingService:
    def __init__(self, pricing_strategy, waitlist_limit):
        self.seats = {}          # seatId -> Seat
        self.bookings = {}       # bookingId -> Booking
        self.waitlists = {SeatClass.ECONOMY: [], SeatClass.BUSINESS: []}  # per-class FIFO queue
        self.capacity = {}        # class -> total seats
        self.waitlist_limit = waitlist_limit  # max waitlisted per class
        self.pricing_strategy = pricing_strategy  # pluggable pricing
        self.observers = []        # listeners
        self.booking_counter = 0   # simple id generator

    def add_seats(self, new_seats):
        for s in new_seats:                                     # register each seat
            self.seats[s.seat_id] = s                              # store by id
            self.capacity[s.seat_class] = self.capacity.get(s.seat_class, 0) + 1  # bump class capacity

    def add_observer(self, observer):
        self.observers.append(observer)  # register a listener

    def _sold_count(self, seat_class):
        count = 0                                                 # running total
        for s in self.seats.values():                              # scan all seats
            if s.seat_class == seat_class and s.status == SeatStatus.BOOKED:
                count += 1                                           # count booked ones
        return count  # total sold in this class

    def book_seat(self, passenger_id, seat_class):
        free_seat = None                                           # will hold a free seat if found
        for s in self.seats.values():                                # scan all seats
            if s.seat_class == seat_class and s.is_available():        # match class and free
                free_seat = s                                           # remember it
                break                                                    # stop at first match
        self.booking_counter += 1                                    # bump id counter
        booking_id = f"BK-{self.booking_counter}"                     # build id
        booking = Booking(booking_id, passenger_id, seat_class)        # build booking
        if free_seat is not None:                                    # a seat is free
            sold = self._sold_count(seat_class)                         # demand before this booking
            fare = self.pricing_strategy.calculate_fare(seat_class, sold, self.capacity[seat_class])  # compute fare
            free_seat.status = SeatStatus.BOOKED                         # claim the seat
            booking.seat_id = free_seat.seat_id                            # link seat
            booking.fare = fare                                              # set fare
            booking.status = "CONFIRMED"                                     # confirmed
            self.bookings[booking_id] = booking                              # store it
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_booking_confirmed(booking)  # notify
            return booking  # hand back to caller
        queue = self.waitlists[seat_class]  # this class's waitlist
        if len(queue) >= self.waitlist_limit:  # waitlist also full
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_booking_cancelled(booking)  # treat as immediately failed
            raise SeatClassFullException(f"No {seat_class} seat or waitlist slot available")
        booking.status = "WAITLISTED"        # waitlisted
        self.bookings[booking_id] = booking   # store it
        queue.append(booking)                  # enqueue FIFO
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_booking_waitlisted(booking)  # notify
        return booking  # hand back to caller

    def cancel_booking(self, booking_id):
        booking = self.bookings.get(booking_id)  # look up booking
        if booking is None or booking.status == "CANCELLED":
            raise BookingNotFoundException(f"Unknown or already-cancelled booking: {booking_id}")
        if booking.status == "WAITLISTED":  # simple case: just dequeue
            self.waitlists[booking.seat_class].remove(booking)  # remove from queue
            booking.status = "CANCELLED"                          # mark cancelled
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_booking_cancelled(booking)  # notify
            return
        seat = self.seats[booking.seat_id]  # the seat this booking held
        seat.status = SeatStatus.AVAILABLE   # free it
        booking.status = "CANCELLED"          # mark cancelled
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_booking_cancelled(booking)  # notify
        queue = self.waitlists[booking.seat_class]  # this class's waitlist
        if queue:                                     # someone is waiting
            promoted = queue.pop(0)                     # longest-waiting entry
            sold = self._sold_count(booking.seat_class)   # demand right now
            fare = self.pricing_strategy.calculate_fare(booking.seat_class, sold, self.capacity[booking.seat_class])  # fresh fare
            seat.status = SeatStatus.BOOKED                # claim the freed seat
            promoted.seat_id = seat.seat_id                  # link seat
            promoted.fare = fare                               # set fare
            promoted.status = "CONFIRMED"                       # confirmed
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_waitlist_promoted(promoted)  # notify

items: Why compute the fare at booking time instead of storing a fixed per-seat price? Because demand-based pricing needs the current sold ratio, which only exists at the moment of the booking attempt.

Why does a promoted waitlist passenger get a freshly computed fare rather than the fare quoted when they joined the waitlist? Because no fare was ever quoted at waitlist time in this design, only a queue position; quoting a fare then honoring it later is a reasonable alternative worth discussing.
How would you support passenger-chosen exact seats? Add an overload that takes a specific seatId and checks only that seat, falling back to the class-based logic if not specified.

First-available seat assignment vs passenger choice: first-available is simpler and faster to book, at the cost of not letting passengers pick window or aisle; a production system would layer choice on top.

Demand-tier pricing vs continuous pricing curve: discrete tiers are easy to reason about and test, while a continuous formula (e.g., exponential in sold ratio) would price more smoothly but is harder to explain to customers.

In-memory synchronized lock vs database transaction: in-memory is fine for a single-process demo; a distributed deployment would need a database-level unique constraint or distributed lock on seat assignment.
Persist seats, bookings, and waitlists in a relational database rather than in-memory maps, using the schema in the Database Design section.
Emit booking/waitlist/cancellation events to a message queue so downstream systems (payments, notifications, analytics) can consume them asynchronously instead of via in-process observers.
Add idempotency keys to bookSeat so retried network requests cannot create duplicate bookings.
Expose metrics on sold ratio per class per flight to guide dynamic pricing tuning and overbooking limits.
